kept_sentences: We report a simulation study planned and reported following Morris, White and Crowther [20], and two clinical applications. || The study has three components. || The first is a simulation over four data-generating mechanisms and a grid that extends to ten clusters and two occasions. || Three mechanisms contain a component that is constant within subject, as the methods compared assume, and the fourth has only serial dependence. || One scenario takes its prevalence and between-subject variance from a neonatal lung-ultrasound cohort. || The second is a recommendation stated as a decision rule that must hold at every simulated design point. || The third is a plasmode application to the cohort and to a public respiratory trial, each repeatedly subsampled into the few-cluster regime with the full-data estimate as reference.<!-- noclaim: aims -->

kept_sentences: 1. GenBinaryY is a marginalized model with a latent variable and a first-order transition term (R package MMLB) [1,2,22]. The latent standard deviation is a linear predictor, which in M3-M5 grows by `r n("x:gby_sigma_m3")` per occasion. This is the mechanism of the marginalized model. || 2. GLMM-native is a logistic mixed model with normal random effects. The random intercept has variance `r n("x:glmm_d11")` and, in M3-M5, the random slope on time has variance `r n("x:glmm_d22")`. The conditional coefficients are the marginal ones multiplied by `r n("x:zeger_f")`. This is the mechanism of the mixed model. || 3. GLMM-AR1 adds a latent first-order autoregressive process to the random effects of GLMM-native (ρ = `r n("x:ar1_rho")`, variance `r n("x:ar1_s2")`). Its random intercept is still constant within subject. || 4. Copula-AR1 is a Gaussian copula with logistic margins. The latent normal scores of a subject have correlation $\rho^{|t_j - t_k|}$, with ρ = `r n("f:x|cop_rho")`, and no component is constant within subject. None of the methods compared assumes this mechanism.

kept_sentences: Each design point received `r n("x:nsim")` replicates per hypothesis. || Replicates in which one treatment arm was never observed after the first occasion were excluded from every denominator (`r n("x:n_degenerate")` per hypothesis in each of the three study mechanisms). || Replicate i of scenario m used the seed `r n("x:seed_rule")` under the L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator. || The seed was the same for both hypotheses and for every N, T and mechanism, so the datasets are common random numbers across cells [20].

The marginalized multilevel model was fitted with `MMLB::mm` (`r n("x:mm_q")` quadrature points), with the latent-variable and transition formulas of the GenBinaryY generator. || GEEs were fitted with `geepack` [23] with exchangeable, independence and first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) working correlations. || They were combined with the uncorrected sandwich variance and with the corrections of Mancl and DeRouen [8], Kauermann and Carroll [9] and Fay and Graubard [10] (bound b = `r n("f:x|fg_bound")`, as in [10]), computed with the R package `fewclust` (Table S2), written for this study and released with the code, which implements the published formulas and agreed with a computation by hand (Section S4). || The CR2 estimator of `clubSandwich` [24,25] was added with exchangeable and independence correlations. || The mixed model was fitted with `lme4::glmer` [26] (Laplace approximation). || After the main run, the mixed model with a random intercept was refitted by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with `r n("f:gq|nodes")` nodes on a subset of null design points (Section 3.10). || It had a random intercept in M1-M2 and the random slopes of the generating model in M3-M5. || It was tested by a Wald test and by a likelihood-ratio test against the model without the interaction, with the same random effects. || The shrinkage GLM rescales the mixed-model estimate and standard error by $(1 + k^2 D_{11})^{-1/2}$, with $D_{11}$ the random-intercept variance. || Its Wald statistic therefore equals that of the mixed model on the same fit; its rejection rate can still differ, because the usability limits of Section 2.5 apply to the rescaled estimate and standard error. || Software versions are in Table S2.

kept_sentences: `MMLB::mm` writes the latent standard deviation as $\exp(a_0) + \exp(a_1)\,t$, so a slope of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space. || In the main scenarios with a latent standard deviation that changes over time (M3-M5), the generating slope is close to that boundary. || Without a check, two failure modes of the optimizer (`nlm`) produced excess rejections with long series: non-convergence with a shifted estimate, and convergence with a collapsed standard error. || We therefore added a convergence check. || A fit was declared at the boundary if `nlm` did not report convergence (return code other than `r n("x:nlm_ok")`) or if an estimated slope $\exp(a_k)$ was below `r n("x:cc_thr")`. || Such a fit was replaced by the fit without the time trend of the latent standard deviation, and kept if that refit failed.<!-- noclaim: definition of the check -->

kept_sentences: Type I error was the rejection rate at the nominal 5% under H0. || Over the grid we report the pooled rate and two summaries computed within each mechanism. || A design point is a combination of scenario, mechanism, number of clusters and number of occasions; a cell is a design point under one hypothesis. || For each of the `r n("x:n_levels_N")` cluster counts we took the absolute departure from 5% of the replicate-weighted rate. || The worst case is the largest of these absolute departures, and the mean absolute departure is their mean. || In the direct comparison of the two strategies of the rule (Section 3.4, Figure 1, Table S31) the absolute departure is instead averaged over design points. || At each design point, a strategy was clearly above 7.5% when the lower limit of the exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% interval of its rejection rate exceeded 7.5%, and clearly below 2.5% when the upper limit fell below 2.5%. || These limits are Bradley's liberal criterion, `r n("f:gt|brad_lo")` to `r n("f:gt|brad_hi")` times the nominal level [28]; for the coverage of 95% intervals they were applied to the rate of non-coverage.<!-- noclaim: definitions --> || Unconditional validity is the probability of a usable result multiplied by the probability of not rejecting a true null given one. || Power was reported raw and size-adjusted. || Bias, empirical and model-based standard errors, root mean squared error and coverage of the 95% interval were computed against the estimand of each method.

Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE) were computed for every measure [20]. || With `r n("x:nsim")` usable replicates, the MCSE of a rejection rate at 5% is `r n("x:mcse_5pct")` percentage points. || This number of replicates was chosen so that a single cell resolves a departure from 5% of about `r n("x:mcse_5pct_2x")` points. || The datasets are common random numbers across cells. || The MCSE of every summary over cells, and of every difference between methods, was therefore obtained by a bootstrap that resamples replicate indices jointly across all cells (`r n("x:boot_B")` resamples). || A comparison between methods is written as a difference only when its bootstrap interval, the estimate ± 2 MCSE, lies entirely beyond a relevance margin fixed in advance. || The margin is one percentage point for differences in type I error or coverage averaged over cells, 2.5 points for a single cell, two points for differences in power and 2.5 points for differences in usable shares. || Intervals entirely within the margin are reported as similar. || Intervals that straddle it are reported as differences of about the size of the margin.<!-- noclaim: definitions -->
